label: Other Important Topics
notes: Open the lecture. Beyond the polynomial and finite type invariants lie several major strands of modern knot theory. The lecture surveys the Alexander polynomial and Seifert surfaces, hyperbolic geometry of knot complements, knot homologies, and the physical origins of quantum invariants, each pointing toward active research.

label: Seifert Surfaces and Genus
notes: Every oriented knot bounds an orientable surface, a Seifert surface, constructed by Seifert's algorithm from any diagram. The least genus among such surfaces is the knot genus, an additive invariant under connected sum. From the surface one reads off the Alexander polynomial via the Seifert matrix and homology of the complement.

label: Hyperbolic Knots
notes: Thurston showed that the complement of most knots admits a complete hyperbolic metric of finite volume. By Mostow rigidity this metric is unique, so its volume and other geometric quantities are honest knot invariants. Hyperbolic geometry classifies knots far more finely than crossing number and connects to deep number theory.

label: Knot Homologies
notes: Categorification replaces a polynomial invariant by a graded homology theory whose Euler characteristic recovers it. Khovanov homology categorifies the Jones polynomial and knot Floer homology categorifies the Alexander polynomial. These richer invariants detect the unknot, bound the genus, and carry information the polynomials alone cannot see.

label: Quantum Invariants and Physics
notes: Witten interpreted the Jones polynomial through Chern-Simons quantum field theory, expressing it as a path integral over connections. This physical picture spawned a whole family of quantum invariants from quantum groups and conformal field theory, and explains the otherwise mysterious appearance of the Jones polynomial in statistical mechanics.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. Seifert surfaces, hyperbolic structures, categorified homologies, and quantum field theory each open a major avenue beyond the elementary invariants. Together they show knot theory as a crossroads of topology, geometry, algebra, and physics. The final lecture places these developments in historical perspective.
